Maladaptive Strategies.value: I pretend it happened to someone else
ruminate about how event could have been prevented
avoid anything that could be stressful

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.

issues.explanation: These items form a combat/interpersonal-violence style hypervigilance pattern centered on armed human threat, which is hard to reconcile with a natural-disaster trauma. A disaster survivor may be generally vigilant, but carrying a weapon and scanning for weapons specifically are not a coherent extension of the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
issues.explanation: The threat profile is narrowly organized around deliberate human attack (weapons, tactical positioning), while the memory items are generic intrusion/detachment phenomena and do not support that specific threat theme. This creates a cross-node mismatch rather than a plausible disaster-related PTSD presentation.

vignette:
Richard is a 74-year-old American man of European background who came to treatment after years of trying to live around an experience he still thinks of as “that storm,” as though putting distance between himself and the words might keep it from becoming immediate again. He lives with his partner and works part-time as a tutor, meeting students in a small learning center and sometimes online. The traumatic event occurred during a severe natural disaster, when a violent storm struck his area and trapped him for hours in a building while the weather raged outside. He remembers the sound first: the prolonged battering of wind and debris, the sense that the structure around him might not hold, and the unnatural waiting as time stretched with no clear idea of when it would end or whether help could reach anyone. The air had its own stamp in his memory too, a damp, splintered smell of soaked wood, mud, and something metallic that he still cannot name without feeling his body tighten.

In the immediate aftermath, Richard found that the event would return to him without warning. He could be doing something ordinary and suddenly the memory would force itself into his mind with a clarity he had not invited. At times he could recall details of the storm in a strangely flat way, with no feeling in his voice, as if he were describing something that had happened to another man entirely. He has noticed this himself and says that sometimes he deals with it by pretending exactly that, that it happened to someone else, because that feels more manageable than letting himself fully register that he was the one there, trapped and waiting. At other moments, though, the memory arrives with sensory force. When he thinks about the storm, he can sometimes smell again the wet, dirty air from that day, and this is often what unsettles him most because it makes the past feel abruptly present.

Over the months and years that followed, Richard became preoccupied with how the disaster might have been prevented. He goes over decisions, warnings, timing, building conditions, routes people did or did not take, circling the same questions about what should have been done differently. He knows there may not be satisfying answers, but his mind returns there anyway. He has also become wary of anything he experiences as stressful, not only obvious reminders of bad weather but situations in general that feel uncertain, pressured, or hard to control. He tries to keep his days predictable and pared down. His partner has noticed that he turns down outings if they seem complicated or potentially tense, and Richard admits that he does this because he feels he has less margin now; if something becomes stressful, he fears his mind will go back to that period of waiting and not knowing.

That sense of danger has come to shape ordinary moments. If something takes longer than expected, his mind quickly jumps to the possibility that something terrible is happening. If his partner is delayed coming home, if a student is late arriving, if an internet connection drops during an online session, Richard does not experience the delay as neutral. He is certain, in those moments, that delay means danger. At the tutoring center he is acutely aware of where he sits. He prefers a chair with his back against the wall and a clear view of the door and the room, and if that is not possible he has trouble focusing on the student in front of him because part of his attention is busy monitoring the space. He scans constantly for signs that something might be wrong. A shift in noise outside, a sudden silence, the movement of people in the hallway, even the feel of the room changing can pull his attention away from teaching. He does not describe this as a choice so much as something he feels compelled to do in order to stay safe.

These habits have narrowed his life in quiet, cumulative ways. He has rearranged where he teaches when he can, and on days when the room setup does not allow him to see everything easily, he comes home exhausted. His partner experiences him as distracted and difficult to reassure when plans change or someone runs late. Richard finds that hard to explain because to him the danger feels obvious in the moment, even when another part of him knows the reaction is bigger than the situation.

He sought help now after a recent interruption during a tutoring session: a student arrived late, there was a delay at the front desk, and while waiting Richard became overwhelmed by the conviction that something bad had happened. The memory of the storm forced itself in, and with it came that same damp smell, so vivid that for a moment the tutoring room no longer felt separate from the building where he had once waited out the disaster. What frightened him most was not only the intensity of that moment but the realization that he has spent years organizing his life around the possibility of it happening again. He says he wants help because he is tired of living as if danger is always about to enter the room, and because he hopes he might still have some years left that are not arranged entirely around fear.
